games.title: On the Books
games.objective: Size the season's cleaning contract by shift, bill it, cost it and judge the margin.
games.study_md: Merrow Facilities cleans 26 sites across the county from 2 regional offices. Through the season it averaged 1,800 operatives on contract. The register at the season's end lists 2,040 operatives. The company has held the county contract since 1971.

analysis.prompt: Day-shift operatives on contract through the season (ex2).

parts.naive_reason: answers with the whole contract staff; ex2 asks for one shift of it

analysis.prompt: Night-shift operatives on contract through the season (ex2).

parts.naive_reason: carries the same mid-point into the second shift: a rising line has an average and an end point, and they are not two readings of one number

analysis.prompt: Season billings, each shift at its own rate (ex2).

parts.naive_reason: bills every operative at the night rate, though night work is barely a third of the contract

analysis.prompt: (a) The season's cost bill (ex2). (b) What share of billings is left as margin.

parts.naive_reason: stops at what the operatives cost to run; the fixed line is owed whoever is on shift
measures the margin against what was spent rather than against what was billed

written.template: Merrow staffed the season at [b1], and the shift that brings in more of the season's billings is [d1]. Day work took [b2] operatives and night work [b3]; between them they billed [b4] dollars against a cost bill of [b5] dollars, leaving [b6] percent as margin.

graph_selection.prompt: Show the season's billings against its cost bill.

cases.prompt: Crossing point — in which month did staffing first reach or pass the level the season averaged?
cases.naive_reason: crosses at the mid-point between the average and the closing register; the line to reach is the season's own average

cases.prompt: Shift swap — if night work rose from 35% to 45% of the same contract staff at the same rates, by how much would season billings move?
cases.naive_reason: bills the operatives who move at the night rate and forgets they stop earning the day rate

cases.prompt: Unit economics — a fixed line of $4,600,000 plus $6,900 of running cost each. What does the season cost for every operative on contract?
cases.naive_reason: answers with the running rate; the fixed line lands on the same operatives and has to be spread over them

cases.prompt: Break-even — billings run at a blended $10,520 an operative against $6,900 of running cost each. How many operatives cover the $4,600,000 fixed line? Round up to a whole operative.
cases.naive_reason: divides the fixed line by the whole billing rate and forgets each operative costs $6,900 to run

cases.prompt: Wage drift — running cost rises by $400 an operative while the rates hold. What is the season margin then, as a share of billings?
cases.naive_reason: puts the rise on the night shift alone; it lands on every operative on contract

cases.prompt: Where does the county's money go further? It offers either 200 more operatives on days at the day rate, or 120 more on nights at the night rate. Running cost is $6,900 either way. Which adds more to the season's MARGIN?
cases.naive_reason: takes the bigger headcount for the bigger gain; each night operative leaves $5,700 against $2,500 on days

analysis_review.lesson: answers with the whole contract staff, not one shift
analysis_review.chain_lesson: took the closing register into the journal: the shift split is being applied to a count from one day, not to the season

analysis_review.lesson: carries the same mid-point into the second shift
analysis_review.chain_lesson: the same closing register carried into the second shift

analysis_review.lesson: bills every operative at the night rate
analysis_review.chain_lesson: billings raised on staff the season never actually carried

analysis_review.lesson: leaves the fixed line out
analysis_review.chain_lesson: running cost charged on a headcount the season never ran

analysis_review.lesson: measures margin against spend, not against billings
analysis_review.chain_lesson: a margin built on the closing register on both sides of the sum

games.title: Running on Empty
games.objective: Size the haulier's season on the kilometres that earn, cost it and judge the margin.
games.study_md: Vardan Haulage runs 26 trucks out of a depot on the Sarel road. Across this season its trucks covered 1,240,000 km with a load on. Counting the runs back to the depot, the fleet covered 1,610,000 km in all. The firm has hauled since 1972.

analysis.prompt: Tonnes carried across the season (ex1).

parts.naive_reason: quotes the busiest quarter as the season; all four quarters carried freight

analysis.prompt: Season haulage revenue (ex2).

parts.naive_reason: puts the haulage rate on the tonnes; the rate is written against distance, not weight

naives.reason: puts the haulage rate on the tonnes; the rate is written against distance, not weight
answers with what the earning kilometres cost to run rather than with what they earned

analysis.prompt: What the season's haulage cost, before fuel (ex2).

parts.naive_reason: counts the depot line alone and leaves out the drivers and wear the kilometres carry

naives.reason: counts the depot line alone and leaves out the drivers and wear the kilometres carry
charges the running cost against tonnes; drivers and wear are written against distance

analysis.prompt: (a) Season profit before fuel. (b) What share of revenue that profit is.

parts.naive_reason: takes the depot line off revenue and never pays the drivers
measures the profit against what was spent; the question asks its share of what came in

written.template: The line that takes more out of Vardan's season is [d1]. The fleet carried [b1] tonnes and billed [b2] dollars against [b3] dollars of haulage cost before fuel, leaving [b4] dollars — [b5] percent of revenue, and fuel is still to come off that. The distance the season is billed on is [b6], and it is not the distance the trucks actually ran.

graph_selection.prompt: Show how the season's tonnage moved across the four quarters.

cases.prompt: Empty running — counting the runs back, the fleet covered 1,610,000 km in all. How many of those kilometres earned nothing?
cases.naive_reason: answers with everything the trucks ran; the runs back are the part of it that no one pays for

cases.prompt: Two offers on the table: cut empty running by a quarter, or lift the haulage rate by 2 cents a kilometre carried. Fuel is $0.34 on every kilometre run. Which puts more into the season?
options: Cut empty running by a quarter
cases.answer: Cut empty running by a quarter
cases.naive_reason: a rate rise touches every earning kilometre and looks wider; the empty quarter is bigger because those kilometres burn fuel and bill nothing

cases.prompt: Revenue per tonne — what did the season's haulage earn for each tonne carried?
cases.naive_reason: divides the season's revenue by a single quarter's tonnes; the revenue was earned across all four

cases.prompt: Fuel on earning work — at $0.34 a kilometre, what did fuel cost on the kilometres that carried a load?
cases.naive_reason: fuels the whole 1,610,000 km; the question asks only about the kilometres that were paid for

cases.prompt: Two ways to lift the season: run the trucks back loaded so that no kilometre goes empty, or carry 5% more kilometres at the same rate. Haulage pays $1.85 a kilometre carried, drivers and wear cost $0.72 on those kilometres, and fuel is $0.34 on every kilometre run. Which puts more into the season?
cases.naive_reason: more work sounds like the bigger move; the runs back burn fuel and bill nothing, and there are six times as many of those kilometres as 5% would add

cases.prompt: All-in cost per earning kilometre — take the haulage cost plus fuel on all 1,610,000 km, and spread it over the kilometres that carried a load.
cases.naive_reason: spreads the all-in cost over every kilometre run; only the carried ones bring the money to cover it

analysis_review.lesson: quotes the busiest quarter as the season
puts the rate on tonnes, not on distance
analysis_review.chain_lesson: took the whole distance run into the journal: the season is billed on the kilometres that carried a load, not on the runs back

analysis_review.lesson: leaves out the drivers and wear
analysis_review.chain_lesson: drivers and wear charged on the empty runs too

analysis_review.lesson: never pays the drivers
analysis_review.chain_lesson: a profit built on distance the customer never paid for

analysis_review.lesson: measures profit against spend, not revenue
analysis_review.chain_lesson: a margin built on the whole distance on both sides of the sum

games.title: Standing Room
games.objective: Work out what a season of ferry crossings was actually worth once concessions are counted.
games.study_md: Kelmar Ferries works 3 quays on the Sarel sound and has sailed since 1964. This season it carried 62,000 paying crossings, and after concessions the average fare it collected was $18.40.

analysis.prompt: Gap between the busiest and the quietest quarter offered (ex1).

parts.naive_reason: answers with the busiest quarter itself; the question asks how far apart the two ends of the season were

analysis.prompt: Season fare revenue.

parts.naive_reason: takes both numbers off the screen — the crossings the boats offered and the fare on the tariff board; neither is what was sold

naives.reason: takes both numbers off the screen — the crossings the boats offered and the fare on the tariff board; neither is what was sold
prices the busiest quarter as the whole season

analysis.prompt: Season profit after the cost lines (ex2).

parts.naive_reason: takes the fixed line off revenue and never pays the fuel and crew each crossing burns

naives.reason: takes the fixed line off revenue and never pays the fuel and crew each crossing burns
pays the crossings but forgets the fixed line the season owes whether the boats sail or not
profit built on the offered crossings AND the board fare — neither of them was sold

analysis.prompt: (a) What share of revenue that profit is. (b) Profit for each paying crossing.

parts.naive_reason: measures the profit against what was spent rather than against what came in

naives.reason: measures the profit against what was spent rather than against what came in
share built on the offered crossings and the board fare together

parts.naive_reason: divides revenue less the fixed line by the crossings and never pays the fuel and crew

naives.reason: divides revenue less the fixed line by the crossings and never pays the fuel and crew
profit per crossing when both numbers come off the screen

written.template: The season collected [b1] a crossing. On that fare the ferries took [b2] dollars and kept [b3] after costs — [b4] percent of revenue. The heavier of the two cost lines is [d1], and every paying crossing left [b5] dollars behind.

options: the fares given away against the tariff board

graph_selection.prompt: Show how the season's revenue divided between cost and what was left.

cases.prompt: Empty seats — the boats offered 74,000 crossings this season. How many of them sailed without paying?
cases.naive_reason: answers with the crossings that paid; the question asks how many of the offered ones did not

cases.prompt: Tariff gap — the board fare is $21.00. Across the season, how much revenue did the concessions give away?
cases.naive_reason: answers with the gap on a single crossing; the season carried that gap on every paying one

cases.prompt: Which took more out of the season — the fares given away against the $21.00 board, or the fuel and crew burned on the crossings that sailed unpaid?
options: Fuel and crew on the unpaid crossings
cases.naive: Fuel and crew on the unpaid crossings
cases.naive_reason: empty seats look like the obvious waste; the concession on every paying crossing runs past what the empty ones burn

cases.prompt: Everything in — the operator also pays $88,000 of harbour dues that sit outside the cost lines above. What share of revenue is left once they are paid?
cases.naive_reason: measures what is left against what was spent; the question asks its share of revenue

cases.prompt: Two offers: fill 6,000 of the unpaid crossings at the fare the season actually collected, or take $60,000 off the fixed cost. Fuel and crew cost $9.60 a crossing. Which is worth more?
cases.naive_reason: filling seats reads as growth; at the fare this season collected a filled crossing leaves $8.80, and six thousand of them fall short of the cut

cases.prompt: Which is bigger over the season — the fuel and crew burned across the paying crossings at $9.60 each, or the $640,000 the operator pays in charter hire?
options: Fuel and crew on the paying crossings
cases.naive: Fuel and crew on the paying crossings
cases.naive_reason: nine dollars sixty on every crossing feels like it must outrun a single printed line; this season it did not, and it only fails to by a margin the crossing count decides

analysis_review.lesson: answers with the busiest quarter instead of the gap
takes both numbers off the screen
